questions.question: A peer answers ICMP, but its BGP session stays Active immediately after TCP-AO was enabled. What should be compared first?
choices: The neighbor's prefix-list order and route-map sequence for this same transaction.
The key ID, algorithm, secret and lifetime on both key-chains.
The BGP hold timer and graceful-restart stale-path interval within the selected policy scope.
The remote peer's advertised networks and next-hop attributes for the same device and service.
feedback: Those controls affect route acceptance after a BGP session forms.
TCP-AO must authenticate the TCP transport before BGP can exchange messages.
Timers do not repair a failed TCP authentication exchange.
Advertised prefixes are unavailable until the peer reaches Established.

questions.question: During a coordinated key rotation, one peer begins sending with a new key before the other accepts it. Which change prevents an avoidable outage?
choices: Increase the BGP keepalive interval on both peers at the receiving system.
Disable TCP-AO until all route filters are synchronized within the selected policy scope.
Create a second neighbor with a different remote AS.
Overlap the receiver's accept lifetime with the sender's new key.
feedback: Keepalive tuning does not resolve a key mismatch.
Disabling authentication removes the intended transport protection.
A duplicate neighbor changes the topology rather than the key transition.
The receiving peer must accept the key before the sender uses it.

questions.question: The TCP-AO diagnostic shows alg=aes128 and matching send/receive IDs. What does this evidence establish?
choices: The TCP-AO key context is active for the displayed peer.
All expected BGP prefixes are installed in the routing table.
The remote peer selected the intended route-map sequence before the next control-plane stage.
The neighbor's next hop is reachable through the preferred WAN.
feedback: Correct: it identifies the peer's algorithm, IDs and key validity context.
It does not show the BGP Adj-RIB-In or installed route set.
Route-map evaluation is a separate BGP policy stage.
Next-hop reachability requires separate routing and forwarding checks.

questions.question: An engineer sets log-max-days to five and Task Monitor rows older than five days disappear after midnight. What is the expected interpretation?
choices: The device configuration revisions were compacted by ADOM cleanup for the same device and service.
The remote FortiAnalyzer deleted the corresponding archived logs before the next control-plane stage.
The local Task Monitor and Event Log age limit was applied.
The completed install jobs were rolled back by scheduled maintenance.
feedback: ADOM revision retention is a separate configuration-history function.
This setting is not a FortiAnalyzer archive-retention command.
Correct: FortiManager truncates local Task Monitor and Event Log records by age.
Log-row removal does not reverse a completed device installation.

questions.question: A FortiManager administrator changes log-max-days from 30 to 0. Which retention behavior returns?
choices: All local task and event records become permanent.
Retention returns to the disk-quota-driven default behavior.
Only failed install tasks are retained until the next reboot.
Task Monitor is disabled while Event Log remains active.
feedback: Zero does not mean unlimited or permanent retention.
Correct: zero restores disk quota as the retention rule.
There is no documented failure-only retention mode here.
The setting does not disable Task Monitor.

questions.question: The audit team needs 90 days of install history, but local disk is constrained. What is the safest design?
choices: Set one day and rely on the task list to reconstruct history.
Set zero and assume the quota guarantees ninety days.
Increase log-max-days without checking local disk capacity at the receiving system.
Export relevant task and event records to approved central storage.
feedback: A one-day window cannot satisfy a 90-day evidence requirement.
Quota-driven retention does not guarantee a fixed age horizon.
A longer age cap does not create additional disk capacity.
Central export preserves evidence independently of local truncation.

questions.question: Chrony receives NTP packets from FortiAnalyzer, but synchronization fails after SHA-256 authentication is enabled. What should be checked first?
choices: The matching key ID and exact key representation on both systems.
The ADOM quota and analytic-to-archive storage ratio at the receiving system.
The FortiAnalyzer report dataset cache and hcache settings within the selected policy scope.
The device log forwarding policy and syslog transport port for the same device and service.
feedback: Correct: key ID, algorithm and hex/ASCII representation must match.
ADOM storage settings do not authenticate NTP messages.
Report caching does not control the NTP client.
Log forwarding is independent of the time-authentication exchange.

questions.question: The FortiAnalyzer uses key ID 123 with a hexadecimal SHA-256 key. Which Chrony entry matches that configuration?
choices: 222 SHA256 somepassword.
123 SHA256 HEX:<matching-hex-key>.
123 MD5 <matching-hex-key>.
123 SHA256 <hex-key-as-ascii-text>.
feedback: The identifier and format do not match the FortiAnalyzer example.
Correct: the same key ID and SHA-256 hex key must be loaded.
The algorithm differs from the configured SHA-256 authentication.
Treating hex text as ASCII changes the key bytes.

questions.question: A packet capture shows bidirectional UDP/123 traffic. What does that observation fail to prove?
choices: That the Chrony server has a route to FortiAnalyzer.
That the NTP client has a configured server object.
That the keyed SHA-256 authentication check succeeded.
That the firewall permits the NTP transport packets.
feedback: The packet exchange supports reachability, not authentication success.
The capture does not show whether the server object is correct.
Correct: a reachable server can still reject a mismatched MAC/key.
The capture indicates that some NTP packets passed the network.

questions.question: A replacement FortiSwitch B rejects an intact backup exported from decommissioned Switch A while verify-config is set to reject. Why is this expected?
choices: The signature proves same-device provenance, and Switch B is not the device that created it
The backup contains a VLAN unsupported by Switch B, so its parser refuses the file
The revision timestamp is older than the replacement switch's current clock value
The management interface address overlaps the backup server's address in the network
feedback: Correct: the signature is bound to the source FortiSwitch, so a different unit cannot verify same-device provenance.
Unsupported configuration syntax is a separate compatibility issue, not the documented signature check.
The timestamp is not the provenance and integrity test described in FortiSwitchOS 8.0.
An address overlap would affect network operation, not the backup signature verifier.

questions.question: A backup generated by a FortiSwitch is edited offline and then restored on that same unit in reject mode. What does the verification failure indicate?
choices: The switch's SNMP trap destination changed during the configuration export
The backup was saved with manual mode instead of automatic configuration save
The archive's compression method is not supported by the current firmware build
The signed file contents no longer match the original device signature
feedback: SNMP settings are configuration content, not the integrity verification mechanism.
Save mode controls when a backup is created, not whether its signed contents were modified.
Compression compatibility would be a different restore/parser failure.
Correct: editing the file breaks the integrity check tied to the original signature.

questions.question: During a controlled cross-device migration, what behavior does FortiSwitchOS verify-config log provide for an unverified backup?
choices: Rejects every backup created manually rather than automatically by the source switch
Accepts the unverified file and records a warning in the system log
Re-signs the imported file with the replacement switch's private signing key
Imports the file but skips all interface and VLAN configuration sections
feedback: The setting is not based on whether the source used manual or automatic save.
Correct: log mode accepts an unverified file and records a warning.
The documented behavior does not silently re-sign foreign files as trusted backups.
The setting does not selectively omit interface and VLAN sections.

questions.question: A tunnel-mode guest SSID completes MAC RADIUS authentication but always sends users to a static portal. Which RADIUS item is missing?
choices: A Class attribute containing the endpoint's IPv4 gateway.
A Called-Station-Id attribute containing the AP radio name.
Fortinet-Captive-Portal-URL vendor attribute 27 in Access-Accept.
A DHCP Option 82 suboption containing the guest VLAN name.
feedback: Class may carry other policy data but is not the documented dynamic URL attribute.
Called-Station-Id identifies the called station, not the portal URL.
Correct: attribute 27 carries the session-specific captive portal URL.
Option 82 is a DHCP relay attribute, not the RADIUS redirect URL.

questions.question: The ISE profile returns attribute 27, but FortiOS does not use the dynamic URL. Which VAP condition should be verified?
choices: Tunnel-mode captive portal with portal-type auth-mac and dynamic redirect enabled.
Bridge-mode SSID with portal-type external-auth and local bridging enabled.
Open SSID with MAC filtering disabled and DHCP relay option 82 enabled.
WPA3 enterprise SSID with EAP-TLS and a static external web address.
feedback: Correct: the feature is enabled on a tunnel-mode captive-portal VAP using auth-mac.
That is a different bridge-mode external-auth workflow.
Those settings do not enable the documented dynamic redirect feature.
EAP-TLS authentication is not the required auth-mac portal mode.

questions.question: Before a guest signs in, the station shows group=unregistered and cp_authed=no. What does this state establish?
choices: The station has completed portal login and Internet access within the selected policy scope.
The station has passed MAC RADIUS authentication but remains unauthenticated to the portal.
The station failed wireless association and has no RADIUS session before the next control-plane stage.
The station has received an authorized VLAN from the DHCP server in this deployment.
feedback: The portal login has not yet completed.
Correct: MAC authentication succeeded, but captive-portal authorization is pending.
The station is online and has a MAC-auth state.
The group/captive-portal fields do not prove DHCP VLAN assignment.

questions.question: A guest reaches the ISE portal and logs in, but cannot browse the Internet. The station is AuthorizedGuest and cp_authed=yes. What is the next check?
choices: The FortiAP channel utilization and radio retry counters for the same device and service.
The ISE dictionary vendor ID and attribute number again.
The RADIUS shared secret rotation interval in this deployment.
The firewall policy allowing the AuthorizedGuest group to the Internet.
feedback: Radio health is not the leading suspect after successful portal login.
The group transition indicates the redirect path already worked.
The shared secret did not prevent the successful authentication exchange.
Correct: post-login traffic requires the authorized-group firewall policy.

questions.question: A laptop disconnects for eight minutes and reconnects without another challenge. Its offline retention timer is ten minutes. Why is this expected?
choices: The prior authenticated state is retained until the offline timer expires.
The reauthentication frequency is disabled on every policy in this deployment.
The production grace timer is restarted whenever a switch is polled.
The RADIUS server cached the password for ten minutes at the receiving system.
feedback: Correct: returning before the offline retention interval ends avoids reauthentication.
The behavior can occur even when periodic reauthentication is configured separately.
Production grace is not the offline retention timer.
The documented behavior is controlled by FortiNAC's policy timer, not a generic RADIUS password cache.

questions.question: A broad catch-all User/Host Profile is placed above a specific contractor profile. Which outcome is most likely?
choices: The contractor profile receives higher precedence because it is narrower.
Both policies are merged and their timers are averaged for this same transaction.
The catch-all matches first and shadows the contractor policy below it.
FortiNAC ignores both policies and uses the portal default within the selected policy scope.
feedback: FortiNAC evaluates policies in order; a later specific rule cannot win.
Policies are not merged into a composite timer configuration.
Correct: first match wins, so the catch-all must be last.
The catch-all is a valid profile match, not an ignored object.

questions.question: RADIUS logs show Access-Accept, but the endpoint is placed in the authentication VLAN. What should be examined next?
choices: The RADIUS shared secret on every network device for this same transaction.
The FortiNAC Policy Details matched profile, configuration and assessment log.
The external directory password expiry policy only within the selected policy scope.
The switch's LLDP neighbor table and PoE budget for the same device and service.
feedback: A valid Access-Accept already shows the identity exchange succeeded.
Correct: NAC policy selection and treatment are a separate decision.
Password expiry may matter to authentication, but the request was accepted.
LLDP and PoE do not explain the selected authentication policy.

questions.question: A user waits too long to authenticate and is moved from production to the authentication VLAN. Which timer controls this transition?
choices: Time Offline before Deauthentication.
Reauthentication Frequency within the selected policy scope.
Time in Production before Authentication.
RADIUS accounting interim-update interval.
feedback: This timer governs retention after the host goes offline.
This timer forces a later reauthentication based on elapsed time since authentication.
Correct: the production grace timer expires and triggers the authentication VLAN move.
Accounting interim updates do not define the VLAN grace period.

questions.question: A host has no matching authentication policy and is deauthenticated after about ten minutes. What design change prevents an undefined policy result?
choices: Create a catch-all profile and place it at the end of the policy list.
Increase the RADIUS server timeout to fifteen minutes for the same device and service.
Disable the authentication VLAN on every managed switch before the next control-plane stage.
Move all user profiles above all host profiles alphabetically in this deployment for this same transaction.
feedback: Correct: Fortinet recommends a catch-all profile/configuration for unmatched hosts.
RADIUS timeout does not create a policy match.
Disabling the authentication VLAN removes a containment mechanism.
Policy ordering is based on first matching profile, not alphabetical grouping.

questions.question: The Entra connector test succeeds, but Windows immediately fails 802.1X. The supplicant is using PEAP while the FortiNAC-F design expects TTLS-PAP. What is the best correction?
choices: Change the Entra tenant ID to the FortiNAC management IP.
Increase the RADIUS retransmit count on the switch.
Disable the Local RADIUS TLS certificate check.
Configure the Windows supplicant for EAP-TTLS with PAP.
feedback: The tenant ID identifies the cloud directory, not the RADIUS server address.
Retransmits do not change the EAP method selected by Windows.
The TLS service is part of the TTLS tunnel and should not be bypassed.
Correct: the client and server must use the same outer EAP method.

questions.question: Why is EAP-TTLS/PAP with Microsoft Entra ID unsuitable when the access policy mandates MFA?
choices: The inner PAP password is sent outside the TLS tunnel.
The documented Entra TTLS-PAP flow does not support MFA.
The FortiSwitch authenticator cannot forward EAP packets for this same transaction.
The Entra service connector only accepts machine certificates.
feedback: PAP is carried inside the outer TTLS-protected tunnel in this design.
Correct: Fortinet explicitly documents the no-MFA limitation.
802.1X authenticators forward EAP through RADIUS in the normal design.
The documented use case supports username/password authentication through Entra.

questions.question: A certificate-based Entra service connector returns Unauthorized. Which distinction is important before replacing the EAP server certificate?
choices: The Entra connector uses the Remote API certificate target, not the Local RADIUS EAP target.
The RADIUS shared secret must be copied into the certificate SAN for this same transaction.
The Windows supplicant must switch from TTLS to open authentication at the receiving system.
The portal FQDN must equal the switch's management IP address within the selected policy scope.
feedback: Correct: the Community case identifies the Remote API certificate target for connector token signing.
A shared secret is not a certificate SAN value.
Open authentication removes the intended EAP security.
The switch management IP does not define the portal certificate identity.

questions.question: An Entra connector poll succeeds, but a user is not in a remote group until after authenticating through FortiNAC. What does this indicate?
choices: The remote group object is corrupted and must be recreated.
The switch is not sending DHCP Option 82 at the receiving system.
Group membership synchronization is separate from the user's authentication event.
The Entra app has no permission to read any user objects.
feedback: The observed behavior is expected in the documented connector workflow.
DHCP relay metadata is unrelated to the Entra group event.
Correct: the successful sync and post-authentication group population are separate stages.
A successful poll does not imply all directory permissions are missing.

questions.question: A new switch is visible as a TACACS+ client, but the intended policy does not match it. What relationship should be inspected?
choices: The switch's SNMP location and sysObjectID values at the receiving system.
The client object's group membership and that group's policy selection.
The RADIUS accounting port and interim-update timer for the same device and service.
The FortiToken push notification setting for local users before the next control-plane stage.
feedback: SNMP inventory data does not select a TACACS+ policy.
Correct: client registration, group membership and policy binding are separate objects.
RADIUS accounting settings do not select TACACS+ clients.
FortiToken push behavior is unrelated to the client-group selector.

questions.question: A TACACS+ client group contains five devices. Which statement remains true about their client identity?
choices: The group replaces all member addresses with one shared subnet.
Every member inherits the group's single shared secret for the same device and service.
The group itself becomes the TACACS+ server identity source before the next control-plane stage.
Each client still requires its own registered address and shared secret.
feedback: The group does not rewrite the individual client addresses.
Client groups are policy selectors, not a shared-secret inheritance model.
Identity source is selected by the TACACS+ policy.
Correct: the group collects existing client objects without replacing them.

questions.question: A policy includes the correct TACACS+ client group, but no request reaches policy evaluation. What should be checked at the appliance first?
choices: Whether TACACS+ service is enabled on the receiving network interface.
Whether the FortiAuthenticator RADIUS client group is empty before the next control-plane stage.
Whether the external switch has an LLDP neighbor entry.
Whether the user account has a default Framed-IP-Address attribute.
feedback: Correct: TACACS+ can be enabled or disabled per FortiAuthenticator interface.
RADIUS group membership is a different service and object type.
LLDP does not enable the TACACS+ listener.
Framed-IP-Address is a RADIUS attribute, not a TACACS+ listener control.

questions.question: An automation script must associate TACACS+ clients with groups through the REST API. Which endpoint family is relevant?
choices: /radiusaccounting/ and /radacctclient/.
/tacplusclientgroups/ and /tacplusgroupclient/.
/samlsp/ and /samlidp/.
/fortitoken/ and /otpusers/.
feedback: These paths do not describe the documented TACACS+ group APIs.
Correct: these endpoints manage TACACS+ client groups and associations.
SAML service-provider endpoints are unrelated to TACACS client grouping.
Token endpoints manage authentication factors, not device groups.

questions.question: An approval request remains pending, but approvers receive no email after switching to Graph. Which diagnostic order best separates the failure domains?
choices: Change the secret's target IP, then restart the RDP proxy.
Recreate the approver role, then disable approval requirements for this same transaction.
Check OAuth token, Graph permission/consent, mailbox access, then FortiPAM notification settings.
Increase the password changer retry count and reset the target password.
feedback: Target IP and RDP proxy settings do not deliver approval notifications.
Approval policy changes could bypass the workflow rather than fix transport.
Correct: token, permission, mailbox authorization and application settings are distinct stages.
Password changer retries are unrelated to approval email delivery.

questions.question: The Graph token request succeeds, but sending to the configured mailbox is denied. Which missing control is most likely?
choices: The Exchange service principal lacks access to the dedicated mailbox.
The FortiPAM secret has no SSH launcher assigned at the receiving system.
The target server is missing a local administrator account.
The FortiPAM approval policy has no time-to-live value for the same device and service.
feedback: Correct: a valid token does not prove mailbox authorization.
SSH launcher assignment does not grant Graph mailbox access.
Target local accounts do not authorize the Microsoft 365 mailbox.
Approval TTL does not control the Graph mailbox permission.

questions.question: Which Microsoft Graph permission and consent step does the FortiPAM 1.9 guide document for the approval mailbox integration?
choices: User.Read delegated permission without tenant consent.
Mail.Send permission on the approver's personal account only.
Directory.Read.All with no mailbox permission.
Mail.ReadWrite with administrator consent.
feedback: The documented integration calls for Mail.ReadWrite, not only User.Read.
The guide specifies Mail.ReadWrite rather than only Mail.Send.
Directory.Read.All does not grant the documented mailbox operation.
Correct: add Mail.ReadWrite and grant admin consent.

questions.question: A Graph email is delivered successfully. What does that prove about the privileged secret request?
choices: The approver has automatically been granted the secret within the selected policy scope.
The email transport worked, but FortiPAM still controls approval state.
The target password was rotated by the email service.
The user has bypassed the secret checkout policy in this deployment.
feedback: Notification delivery does not approve the underlying request.
Correct: approval state remains in the FortiPAM workflow.
Graph email delivery does not change target credentials.
The notification path does not bypass checkout policy.

questions.question: A Windows certificate expires, but no FortiSIEM event appears. The template exists. What should be verified next?
choices: The Windows firewall default route and DNS suffix.
The event correlation rule severity and notification recipient.
The Host-to-Template Association and whether Apply distributed it.
The FortiGate SSL inspection profile on the endpoint subnet.
feedback: Host network settings are not the first template-delivery check.
A correlation rule cannot process an event that never arrived.
Correct: the template must be attached to the host and applied.
SSL inspection does not enable the Windows Agent certificate watcher.

questions.question: Which event type indicates that a monitored Windows certificate store contains a certificate approaching its configured expiry threshold?
choices: AO-WUA-Certificate-Expiring.
AO-WUA-Certificate-Removed.
AO-WUA-Certificate-Added.
AO-WUA-Certificate-Expired.
feedback: Correct: Expiring is the advance-warning event.
Removed reports deletion from the monitored store.
Added reports insertion into the monitored store.
Expired reports that the certificate has already expired.

questions.question: A certificate-removed event appears for LocalMachine. What conclusion is justified from that event alone?
choices: The certificate chain was untrusted by every application.
The private key was compromised and exported for this same transaction.
The service binding was automatically moved to another certificate.
The agent detected removal from the configured certificate store.
feedback: Store removal does not establish trust-chain status.
The event does not prove private-key compromise or export.
The event does not report application service-binding changes.
Correct: the event records the configured store operation.

questions.question: The Windows Agent is installed and online, but certificate events are absent. Which configuration belongs on the FortiSIEM side?
choices: A separate Windows scheduled task for each certificate store.
A monitor template with stores/operations and a host association.
A new SNMP trap receiver for the Windows certificate service.
A custom parser for every certificate issuer's subject name.
feedback: Fortinet documents template-based monitoring rather than per-store scheduled tasks.
Correct: select certificate stores/operations, associate the host and Apply.
Certificate events are collected by the agent, not by SNMP traps.
A parser is not required to enable the documented event source.

questions.question: A subnet-based ZTNA private application is configured, but endpoints run FortiClient Windows 7.2.7. What is the immediate compatibility issue?
choices: Range/CIDR and port-list support requires Windows FortiClient 7.2.8 or later.
The ZTNA gateway must use UDP port 1812 for every application.
The application must be converted to an agentless custom domain.
The FortiGate gateway must disable all SAML authentication before the next control-plane stage.
feedback: Correct: the documented minimum for range/CIDR and port lists is 7.2.8.
RADIUS UDP/1812 is not the ZTNA application-gateway transport requirement.
Agentless ZTNA is a separate access mode.
SAML authentication is configurable and not universally disabled.

questions.question: The private application object is visible in FortiSASE, but traffic still bypasses the intended ZTNA rule. What binding is missing?
choices: A DHCP reservation for the application subnet within the selected policy scope.
A BGP route-map on the Security PoP for the same device and service.
A ZTNA connection rule in the endpoint profile referencing that application.
A FortiAnalyzer report dataset for the application gateway in this deployment.
feedback: DHCP reservation does not deploy a ZTNA application policy.
A BGP route-map does not bind the application to FortiClient.
Correct: the endpoint profile must reference the private application.
A report dataset is not part of endpoint policy distribution.

questions.question: An administrator enables ZTNA encryption. Which traffic leg does this setting control?
choices: The original server-to-database traffic inside the private subnet.
The FortiClient-to-ZTNA-application-gateway connection.
The Entra ID OAuth token exchange between cloud services.
The IPsec tunnel between two unrelated branch FortiGates.
feedback: The setting does not change application-server internal traffic.
Correct: it controls encryption between FortiClient and the gateway.
OAuth token transport is a separate identity exchange.
Unrelated branch tunnels are not controlled by this endpoint-profile option.

questions.question: An enterprise is approaching the documented ZTNA connection-rule ceiling. Which limit should guide design review?
choices: 3,200 private application objects across all tenants.
320,000 gateway connections per FortiGate.
32,000 ZTNA connection rules in FortiSASE.
320 ZTNA rules per endpoint profile.
feedback: The documented rule limit is higher than 3,200.
This is not the published FortiSASE rule limit.
Correct: FortiSASE documents a maximum of 32,000 ZTNA connection rules.
The limit is not 320 rules per profile.

questions.question: A spoke uses route-metric priority. Which SLA values drive the BGP MED mapping?
choices: The member's priority-in-sla and priority-out-sla values.
The BGP hold timer and keepalive multiplier.
The overlay interface MTU and TCP MSS clamp.
The hub's local preference and route-reflector cluster ID.
feedback: Correct: priority mode maps the member's SLA priority values.
BGP timers do not encode the SD-WAN member priority.
MTU/MSS settings do not define the MED mapping.
Those are separate BGP attributes and control-plane settings.

questions.question: A design wants the BGP neighbor selected according to health-check preferable/unpreferable route-map behavior. Which route-metric mode matches that intent?
choices: priority.
lowest-cost.
preferable.
round-robin.
feedback: Priority uses member priority-in-sla/out-sla values.
Lowest-cost is not the documented route-metric option here.
Correct: preferable follows the health-check result for route-map matching.
Round-robin is not the documented BGP route-metric mode.

questions.question: Both hubs advertise the same spoke prefix, but the external router selects Hub-2 despite Hub-1 having a lower MED. What should be examined?
choices: The FortiAP radio channel plan and DFS state.
The FortiNAC host registration VLAN within the selected policy scope.
The external router's higher-precedence BGP attributes and policy.
The FortiManager task monitor retention window before the next control-plane stage.
feedback: Wireless radio settings do not determine the external BGP best path.
NAC VLAN state is unrelated to route selection.
Correct: local preference and other earlier decision criteria can outrank MED.
Log retention cannot change BGP path selection.

questions.question: The spoke's health-check output shows a healthy overlay. What additional evidence is required to prove the intended MED reached the external network?
choices: The hub's advertised-routes output for the spoke prefix.
The spoke's wireless station table for the same device and service.
The FortiAnalyzer NTP synchronization status before the next control-plane stage.
The FortiPAM approval email delivery log in this deployment.
feedback: Correct: inspect the route and Metric on the hub/external BGP advertisement.
Wireless state is not evidence of BGP attribute propagation.
NTP status is unrelated to route advertisement.
Approval email logs do not prove BGP MED propagation.

questions.question: The neighbor's member list omits the overlay that should carry the preferred path. What is the likely effect?
choices: The external router will infer the missing member from its AS path.
The MED mapping cannot reflect the omitted member's SLA priority.
The hub will automatically create a new iBGP neighbor for that member.
The health-check will rewrite the spoke's route distinguisher for this same transaction.
feedback: BGP does not infer an omitted SD-WAN member from AS_PATH.
Correct: only selected members participate in the neighbor's mapping.
A missing member does not automatically create a BGP neighbor.
The health-check does not rewrite route distinguishers.

questions.question: FortiGate TCP-AO diagnostics show a valid authenticated peer, while BGP advertises no expected prefixes. Which investigation boundary is correct?
choices: Continue changing the TCP-AO key until prefixes appear.
Treat the authenticated transport as proof of correct route policy.
Disable BGP authentication and rebuild the neighbor from scratch.
Move to BGP address-family, policy and route-selection verification.
feedback: A valid transport does not imply route policy is correct.
TCP-AO proves transport authentication, not prefix acceptance.
Disabling authentication does not diagnose missing route advertisements.
Correct: troubleshoot BGP after the transport is authenticated.

questions.question: A FortiNAC user passes RADIUS authentication, and a FortiSIEM certificate event is present. Which evidence should not be conflated?
choices: RADIUS identity acceptance versus FortiNAC network-access policy decision.
Certificate expiry event versus Windows certificate store selection.
FortiSIEM collector receipt versus correlation-rule execution at the receiving system.
FortiNAC host role versus authentication configuration timer.
feedback: Correct: successful identity authentication does not determine NAC VLAN treatment.
These are related but separate monitoring stages.
Collector receipt and rule execution are distinct.
Host role and timer configuration are separate policy inputs.

questions.question: A key-chain entry exists on both BGP peers, but one peer's accept-lifetime expired yesterday. What is the likely result?
choices: The receiver may reject segments using that key despite the key still appearing in configuration.
The receiver will accept the key until the BGP hold timer expires at the receiving system.
The sender will automatically select a route-map with matching lifetime within the selected policy scope.
The peer will keep the TCP session and only suppress IPv4 UPDATE messages for the same device and service.
feedback: Correct: the receive key must be within its accept lifetime when the peer authenticates traffic.
The BGP hold timer is not a substitute for key acceptance validity.
Route-map selection is unrelated to key-chain lifetime.
TCP-AO failure affects the transport, not only one address family.

questions.question: After authenticated NTPv4 is working, which security property has SHA-256 keyed authentication added?
choices: Confidentiality of the time payload against passive packet capture.
Encryption of all FortiAnalyzer log records before storage.
Mutual authentication of every device sending logs to FortiAnalyzer.
Integrity and origin authentication of the NTP time messages.
feedback: NTP keyed authentication does not hide the time payload.
The setting does not encrypt stored logs.
Log-source authentication is a separate ingestion/security control.
Correct: the shared key authenticates the time message and protects its integrity.
